title: A prior decree fixing all connections of possibles is fiction, idle, and unworthy of God's goodness and justice
source_text: LII. Imo etiam plane commentitium, neque tantum sapientiae, sed etiam divinae bonitati repugnans videtur illud decretum quo nonnulli volunt, ut supra retulimus, Deum omnium fieri possibilium connexiones & concatenationes apud se praefinivisse, priusquam decerneret aliquid esse futurum. Nam si ita esset, oporteret ut Deus, antequam hunc mundum creare statueret, hujusmodi decreta apud se concepisset, si velim Adamum creare, volo ut ejus lapsus cum ejus tentatione necessario cohaereat. Si velim creare Davidem & illum videre Bathscebah, volo ut cum isto visu connexa sit istius mulieris concupiscentia. Item, volo ut tales occasiones peccandi consequantur talia peccata, si decernam tales occasiones fore. Imo volo ut in infinitis mundis a me creabilibus hi & illi eventus contingenter possibiles cum his & illis ejusdem naturae eventibus nexum habeant inseparabilem. Quae certe decreta non tantum plane otiosa, frivola & frustranea sunt, sed maxime dedecent bonitatem & justitiam illius qui Deus nolens iniquitatem est.
pass_a_gloss: LII. Nay also that decree seems plainly fictitious, and repugnant not only to wisdom, but also to the divine goodness, by which some will, as we related above, that God predefined with himself the connections and concatenations of all things possible to be made, before he decreed anything to be future. For if it were so, it would be necessary that God, before he resolved to create this world, should have conceived with himself decrees of this kind, if I will to create Adam, I will that his fall cohere necessarily with his temptation. If I will to create David and him to see Bathsheba, I will that with that sight be connected the concupiscence of that woman. Likewise, I will that such occasions of sinning be followed by such sins, if I decree that such occasions shall be. Nay I will that in infinite worlds creatable by me these and those events contingently possible have an inseparable nexus with these and those events of the same nature. Which decrees certainly are not only plainly idle, frivolous and vain, but most greatly misbecome the goodness and justice of him who is a God not willing iniquity.
pass_b_english: Indeed, the decree some posit, as reported above, by which God fixed within himself the connections and sequences of everything that could be made before he decreed anything to be future, seems pure invention. It seems contrary not only to God's wisdom but also to his goodness.

If it were so, God would have had to form decrees like these within himself before resolving to create this world: 'If I will to create Adam, I will that his fall be necessarily bound up with his temptation. If I will to create David and that he see Bathsheba, I will that lust for that woman be joined to that sight.'

Or again: 'I will that such occasions of sin be followed by such sins, if I decree that such occasions shall exist.' Or even: 'I will that in the countless worlds I could create, these or those contingently possible events be inseparably linked with these or those events of the same kind.'
Such decrees are not only plainly idle, trivial and pointless. They are utterly unworthy of the goodness and justice of the one who is a God who does not will iniquity.
